findings.safety_implication: Small, low-heat-loss fires are the persistent ones - they can smoulder unnoticed in still air.

findings.question: Q2: How big / fast does a spacecraft fire get, and what does it do to cabin air?
findings.material_or_fuel: nylon netting, Velcro, polyurethane foam, ECU insulation
findings.condition: sealed Command Module, 100% O2 at 16.7 psia, crew suited, pad test
findings.value: cabin ruptured ~15 s after first crew fire report (~36 psi)
findings.finding: In the 1967 Apollo 1 ground test, fire in the sealed 100% oxygen cabin spread over nylon netting, Velcro and ECU insulation; about 15 s after the crew first reported fire, cabin pressure reached ~36 psi and the hull ruptured. All three crew members died.
findings.safety_implication: In a high-oxygen cabin a small ignition can become a cabin-wide fire within seconds, faster than the crew can escape.
findings.source_file: NTRS 19820066930 - Report of Apollo 204 Review Board (1967) https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19820066930/downloads/19820066930.pdf
findings.caveat: Real incident, not a controlled experiment: 1-g launch-pad ground test in a sealed cabin; the Board could not conclusively identify the ignition source. Page = PDF page (printed report page in brackets).
findings.quote: At approximately 6:31:19, the internal pressure had risen to an estimated 36 pounds per square inch and the sealed cabin ruptured.

findings.question: Q1: Which materials burn most easily (incl. exploration atmospheres)?
findings.material_or_fuel: nylon, polyurethane foam, Velcro and other cabin combustibles
findings.condition: 100% O2 at 16.7 psia, combustibles next to possible ignition sources
findings.finding: The Apollo 204 Review Board found many combustible materials next to possible ignition sources in a 16.7 psia, 100% oxygen atmosphere and judged the test conditions extremely hazardous. No single ignition source was conclusively identified; the most probable initiator was an electrical arc near Environmental Control System wiring.
findings.safety_implication: Restricting the amount and placement of flammable materials is a primary fire defence, especially in oxygen-enriched atmospheres such as the proposed 34% O2 exploration atmosphere.
findings.source_file: NTRS 19820066930 - Report of Apollo 204 Review Board (1967) https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19820066930/downloads/19820066930.pdf
findings.caveat: Real incident, not a controlled experiment: 1-g launch-pad ground test in a sealed cabin; the Board could not conclusively identify the ignition source. Page = PDF page (printed report page in brackets).
findings.quote: The amount and location of combustible materials in the Command Module must be severely restricted and controlled.

findings.question: Q2: How big / fast does a spacecraft fire get, and what does it do to cabin air?
findings.condition: inside high-pressure cryogenic O2 tank; insulation heat-damaged (~1000 F) during ground detanking
findings.value: wire-insulation fire failed the tank; mission aborted
findings.finding: On Apollo 13, thermostatic switches rated for 28 V failed on 65 V ground power, letting heaters reach about 1000 F and damage Teflon insulation on fan-motor wires inside oxygen tank no. 2. About 56 hours into the flight the wiring short-circuited and ignited its insulation; the combustion failed the tank, blew off a service-module panel and aborted the Moon landing.
findings.safety_implication: Wiring and motors in contact with high-pressure oxygen are ignition hazards; hidden damage from ground testing can stay dormant until flight.
findings.source_file: NTRS 19700076776 - Report of Apollo 13 Review Board (1970) https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19700076776/downloads/19700076776.pdf
findings.caveat: Real incident, not a controlled experiment: the fire was inside a high-pressure cryogenic oxygen tank, not in cabin air, so cabin O2/pressure are left blank. Page = PDF page (printed report page in brackets).
findings.quote: the fan motor wiring, possibly moved by the fan stirring, short circuited and ignited its insulation by means of an electric arc.

findings.question: Q1: Which materials burn most easily (incl. exploration atmospheres)?
findings.material_or_fuel: Teflon, aluminum and other relatively combustible materials
findings.condition: in contact with oxygen and potential ignition sources (oxygen storage system)
findings.value: minimise combustibles in oxygen systems; research combustion at various g levels
findings.finding: After Apollo 13 the Review Board recommended removing wiring and unsealed motors from contact with oxygen, minimising Teflon, aluminum and other relatively combustible materials near oxygen and ignition sources, and more NASA research on ignition and combustion in strong oxidizers at various g levels.
findings.safety_implication: Materials that are hard to ignite in air can burn in pure or high-pressure oxygen; oxygen-system materials need testing under the actual oxygen and gravity conditions.
findings.source_file: NTRS 19700076776 - Report of Apollo 13 Review Board (1970) https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19700076776/downloads/19700076776.pdf
findings.caveat: Real incident, not a controlled experiment: the fire was inside a high-pressure cryogenic oxygen tank, not in cabin air, so cabin O2/pressure are left blank. Page = PDF page (printed report page in brackets).
findings.quote: Minimize the use of Teflon, aluminum, and other relatively combustible materials in the presence of the oxygen and potential ignition sources.
